summary: Mobbin interviews Jonathan Parra, who has designed over 4,700 paywalls for consumer apps, about what to test on a subscription paywall and in what order. He says a first paywall only needs a headline, a couple of bullet points and a continue button, and that radically different designs move results most, followed by personalization, then how the products and prices are packaged in the footer, with device-based pricing as a late, costly lever. He argues the right success metric depends on the business: ARPU for a quick launch, LTV and retention for a long-term business, because high ARPU from weekly plans can hide very high churn. He covers paywall touch points (after onboarding, feature gates, settings, cancellation and deletion), account creation before the paywall, when steep discounts help or cannibalize revenue, and why he dislikes spin-the-wheel paywalls. For a design system this is guidance on the paywall pattern and its variants rather than on visual tokens [inferred].
key_ideas: Paywall optimization matters little at the start; get users into the app first and optimize that traffic later.
A first paywall can be just a headline describing the product, a couple of bullet points on what it does, and a continue button.
Radically different paywall designs (video, bullet list, trial timeline, long-form) move results more than anything else, so test those first.
After design, personalization matters most: the user's name, their goals and imagery that reflects their identity.
Price packaging comes next: how the footer lays out the products and how each price is presented.
Default to the yearly product for its higher LTV and show only two products to reduce cognitive load, while checking that yearly suits your business.
Device-based pricing tests are among the last levers because they take so much work for smaller gains.
ARPU alone can mislead; weekly plans can raise ARPU while monthly churn runs very high.
Choose the key metric by the kind of business: ARPU for a quick launch, LTV and retention for a long-term business.
The share of installs that see the paywall is a health check: above 80% is good, 90% or above is excellent.
Run the current paywall as a control against four to five new designs, and be patient because wins are not guaranteed.
Every touch point deserves testing, but the after-onboarding paywall is the most used.
Steep discounts fit win-back moments for subscribers about to cancel, not the first paywall after onboarding.
Spin-the-wheel discount paywalls can raise short-term revenue but teach users to close paywalls and wait for an offer.
The highest converting paywall is not always the right one; it depends on what kind of business you are building.

rules.rule: Ship a first paywall with just a headline describing the product, a couple of bullet points on what it does, and a continue button; do not start with heavy optimization.
rules.why: In the beginning you only need to get users into the app; the traffic can be optimized later.
rules.evidence: [0:26] For your first paywall, honestly, all that you need

rules.rule: Test radically different paywall designs (for example a video paywall, a bullet list paywall, a trial timeline paywall and a long-form paywall) before testing smaller details.
rules.why: Design tests move the needle the most; keep trying until one design blows everything else out of the water.
rules.evidence: [0:52] Design tests move the needle the most

rules.rule: After the design is settled, personalize the paywall: call out the user's name, highlight their goals and show imagery that represents their identity.
rules.why: After design, personalization moves the needle the most.
rules.evidence: [1:04] After design, personalization moves the needle the most

rules.rule: Preselect the yearly product in the paywall footer by default, after checking that a yearly plan suits your business.
rules.why: The yearly product shows the highest LTV, but it may not be the best for every business.
rules.evidence: [1:39] Ideally, you want to default to a yearly product

rules.rule: Show only two products on the paywall, for example a yearly and a weekly plan.
rules.why: Two options decrease cognitive load on the user.
rules.evidence: [1:46] You only want to show two to decrease cognitive load

rules.rule: Leave device-based price tests (such as a higher price for newer phones on fast networks) until design, personalization and price packaging have been tested.
rules.why: It is one of the last levers because it is so much work, and each later lever moves the needle less.
rules.evidence: [2:19] that's like one of the last levers that you really pull

rules.rule: Do not judge a paywall experiment by ARPU alone; also check paywall percentage, trial to paid conversion rate, LTV, D1, D7, D30 and churn.
rules.why: ARPU can look high because of weekly products while churn is 90 to 95% per month, so it does not tell the full picture.
rules.evidence: [2:37] ARPU doesn't necessarily give you all the answers

rules.rule: Track the share of installs that actually see the paywall and aim for above 80%.
rules.why: Above 80% is doing well; 90% or above is crushing it.
rules.evidence: [2:55] I typically look at paywall percentage

rules.rule: Pick the key paywall metric by business type: ARPU for an app built to launch and gain as many users as possible, LTV and retention for a long-term business.
rules.why: A long-term business wants to maximize revenue while still balancing churn.
rules.evidence: [3:15] If you're vibe coding an app ... ARPU as the key metric

rules.rule: Use the current paywall as the control and test four to five new paywall designs against it, and keep experimenting if the first round does not win.
rules.why: Most clients beat the control in the first week, but some needed a second or third experiment to reach a statistically significant win.
rules.evidence: [3:37] We take your paywall and use that as a control

rules.rule: Design and test paywalls for every touch point: after onboarding, gated features, the settings page, account cancellation and before the user deletes the app.
rules.why: All the different touch points are extremely important.
rules.evidence: [4:08] All the different touch points are extremely important

rules.rule: Show a paywall right after onboarding.
rules.why: It is the most used paywall; 78% of iOS apps on Mobbin show the paywall after onboarding.
rules.evidence: [4:30] the most used paywall, it's the after onboarding paywall

rules.rule: Consider creating the account before showing the paywall, and test the order in your own app category.
rules.why: Account first ties a user ID to the person subscribing; the guest's own tests of the order were inconclusive across categories.
rules.evidence: [4:53] I like to create an account first and then show the paywall

rules.rule: Do not show a steep discount such as 80% off immediately after onboarding.
rules.why: It can cannibalize revenue before users have even had a chance to see the paywall a few more times.

rules.rule: When a subscriber wants to cancel, show a win-back paywall with a discounted offer; a steep discount is acceptable there.

rules.evidence: [5:10] Having a steep discount in your win back campaign, I think is okay

rules.rule: Avoid predetermined spin-the-wheel discount paywalls when building a long-term business.

rules.evidence: [5:50] If you're optimizing for the longer-term business, that may not be a good paywall for you

options.name: Personalization

process.detail: Start with a headline describing the product, a couple of bullet points on what it does and a continue button; focus on getting users into the app.
Use the existing paywall as the control and design four to five paywalls to test against it.
Try video, bullet list, trial timeline and long-form paywalls until one clearly beats the rest.
Call out the user's name, highlight their goals and show imagery representative of the user's identity.
Test the footer: vertical or horizontal product groups, what goes in each, how the price is presented, a yearly default and only two products.
Test prices by device, network and battery state only after the bigger levers, because it is a lot of work.
Check paywall percentage, trial to paid, LTV, D1, D7, D30 and churn, and use ARPU as the key metric only for a quick launch.
If the first experiment does not produce a statistically significant win, run a second or third.
Add and test paywalls after onboarding, at feature gates, in settings, on cancellation with a win-back offer and before app deletion.

examples.visual_note: For a male user the paywall shows a strong man, so the image represents the user's identity.
A yearly and a weekly product, each shown as a weekly price with a subtitle giving the actual real price; raised as a presentation to test, not a recommendation.
A user on an iPhone 17 Pro on 5G without low battery mode sees a higher price; a user on an iPhone 13 Pro on 3G with low battery sees a lower price.
A paywall shown when the user is about to delete the app, with copy like "Before you go ... we'd love for you to try one last time."
A subscriber who wants to cancel is shown a discounted offer to keep them.
A predetermined wheel-spin lottery that lands on a discount percentage; shown as a practice the guest disagrees with.

caveats: This is an interview on Mobbin's channel with a paywall consultant whose site (tapasgrowth.com) is linked; his claim that his team beat the control in the first week for every client except two is self-reported and unverified.
The 78% after-onboarding figure is Mobbin's own count of iOS apps in its library, not an industry-wide measure.
The advice is from one practitioner's experience with consumer subscription apps; he says his account-before-paywall tests were inconclusive, so treat that part as preference.
Device names (iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 13 Pro) date the device-based pricing example to 2026; the source does not discuss the fairness of charging different prices by device [inferred].
The guest says spin-the-wheel paywalls do work for weekly-price revenue; his objection is about long-term business, not effectiveness.
Auto-captions: "lottery file" at [5:48] is probably a mis-hearing, and a gap between [3:30] and [3:37] suggests an edit in the interview [inferred].
The video description is truncated ("Previously, he worked at S"), so the guest's background is incomplete.
